questions.question: Let $*$ be the binary operation on $\mathbb{Z}^{+}$, defined by $a*b=|a-b|$. Find the value of $3*7$.
questions.answer: The definition is $a*b=|a-b|$, so put $a=3$ and $b=7$:$$3*7=|3-7|=|-4|$$$$=4$$$$\therefore\ 3*7=4$$The operation simply returns the (non-negative) distance between the two integers. Note it is **commutative** ($3*7=7*3=4$) but not a group operation on $\mathbb{Z}^{+}$, since $3*3=0\notin\mathbb{Z}^{+}$ — which is exactly why this topic sits in the deleted portion of the syllabus.

questions.question: Evaluate $\sin\left\{\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac12\right)\right\}$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — pull the minus sign out of $\sin^{-1}$.** Since $\sin^{-1}$ is odd, $\sin^{-1}(-x)=-\sin^{-1}x$:$$\sin^{-1}\left(-\frac12\right)=-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)=-\frac{\pi}{6}$$(because $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac12$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\in\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ ✓).**Step 2 — substitute inside the bracket:**$$\frac{\pi}{3}-\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{2\pi+\pi}{6}=\frac{3\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{2}$$**Step 3 — take the sine:**$$\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=1$$$$\therefore\ \sin\left\{\frac{\pi}{3}-\sin^{-1}\left(-\frac12\right)\right\}=1$$

questions.question: Find the values of $x$ and $y$, where $\begin{bmatrix}2x+y&3y\\ 6&4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}6&0\\ 6&4\end{bmatrix}$.
questions.answer: Two matrices are equal when every corresponding entry is equal. Comparing:**From the $(1,2)$ entry:**$$3y=0\ \Rightarrow\ y=0$$**From the $(1,1)$ entry:**$$2x+y=6$$With $y=0$:$$2x+0=6\ \Rightarrow\ x=3$$The remaining entries ($6=6$, $4=4$) are automatically satisfied.$$\therefore\ x=3,\qquad y=0$$**Check:** $2(3)+0=6$ ✓ and $3(0)=0$ ✓.

questions.question: Find the minors of all the elements of $\begin{bmatrix}2&-4\\ 0&3\end{bmatrix}$.
questions.answer: For a $2\times2$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{bmatrix}$ the minor of an entry is the determinant left after deleting its row and column:- Minor of $a_{11}=2$: delete row 1 and column 1, leaving $[3]$, so $M_{11}=|3|=3$- Minor of $a_{12}=-4$: leaving $[0]$, so $M_{12}=|0|=0$- Minor of $a_{21}=0$: leaving $[-4]$, so $M_{21}=|-4|=-4$- Minor of $a_{22}=3$: leaving $[2]$, so $M_{22}=|2|=2$$$\therefore\ M_{11}=3,\quad M_{12}=0,\quad M_{21}=-4,\quad M_{22}=2$$(In a $2\times2$ matrix each minor is just the diagonally opposite entry — a useful shortcut. Note that for the symmetrically placed pairs $M_{11}=M_{22}$ is *not* generally true; here it happens only by chance.)

questions.question: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$ at the point $(-3,4)$.
questions.answer: Differentiate the implicit equation with respect to $x$:$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^{2}\right)+\frac{d}{dx}\left(y^{2}\right)=0$$$$2x+2y\frac{dy}{dx}=0$$$$\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{y}$$At $(-3,4)$:$$\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(-3,4)}=-\frac{-3}{4}=\frac34$$$$\therefore\ \text{slope of the tangent}=\frac34$$**Geometric check:** the curve is the circle of radius $5$ centred at the origin; the radius to $(-3,4)$ has slope $\dfrac{4}{-3}=-\dfrac43$, and $\dfrac34\times\left(-\dfrac43\right)=-1$ ✓ — tangent perpendicular to the radius, as it must be.

questions.question: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ if $y=\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x$.
questions.answer: Use the identity valid for **every** real $x$:$$\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}$$So $y=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, a constant independent of $x$, and$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$$$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=0$$**The same result by direct differentiation** (a good cross-check):$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}-\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}=0\ ✓$$The two inverse functions have derivatives that are exact negatives of each other, which is the calculus face of the identity.

questions.question: Solve: $\displaystyle\int a^{3\log_{a}x}\,dx$.
questions.answer: First simplify the integrand using the fundamental identity of logarithms. If $y=a^{3\log_{a}x}$ then$$\log_{a}y=3\log_{a}x=\log_{a}\left(x^{3}\right)\ \Rightarrow\ y=x^{3}$$Equivalently, $a^{\log_{a}t}=t$, so$$a^{3\log_{a}x}=\left(a^{\log_{a}x}\right)^{3}=x^{3}$$Now integrate the power function:$$\int x^{3}\,dx=\frac{x^{4}}{4}+C$$$$\therefore\ \int a^{3\log_{a}x}\,dx=\frac{x^{4}}{4}+C$$(Valid for $x>0$, where $\log_{a}x$ is defined; the $a$'s cancel out completely, so the answer does not depend on the base $a$.)

questions.question: For what value of $p$ are the vectors $3\hat i+2\hat j+9\hat k$ and $\hat i+p\hat j+3\hat k$ parallel?
questions.answer: Two vectors are parallel exactly when their cross product vanishes (equivalently, when their components are proportional).With $\vec a=3\hat i+2\hat j+9\hat k$ and $\vec b=\hat i+p\hat j+3\hat k$:$$\vec a\times\vec b=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 3&2&9\\ 1&p&3\end{vmatrix}$$$$=\hat i\left(6-9p\right)-\hat j\left(9-9\right)+\hat k\left(3p-2\right)$$$$=\left(6-9p\right)\hat i+0\hat j+\left(3p-2\right)\hat k$$For $\vec a\times\vec b=\vec 0$ both components must vanish:$$6-9p=0\ \Rightarrow\ p=\frac{6}{9}=\frac23$$$$3p-2=0\ \Rightarrow\ p=\frac23\ ✓\ \text{(consistent)}$$$$\therefore\ p=\frac23$$**Proportional-components check:** $\dfrac{3}{1}=\dfrac{2}{p}=\dfrac{9}{3}=3$, so $p=\dfrac23$ ✓ — the two vectors are $(3,2,9)=3(1,p,3)$.

questions.question: Find the order and degree of the differential equation $\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{4}+3\dfrac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}=0$.
questions.answer: **Order** = order of the highest derivative present. The derivatives are $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ (order 1) and $\dfrac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}$ (order 3), so$$\text{order}=3$$**Degree** = the power of the highest-order derivative, after the equation is cleared of radicals and fractions in the derivatives. Here the highest-order derivative $\dfrac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}$ appears to the first power, so$$\text{degree}=1$$$$\therefore\ \text{order}=3,\qquad \text{degree}=1$$**Careful trap:** the fourth power belongs to $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, which is *not* the highest-order derivative, so it plays no part in the degree. (This is why degree must always be read off the highest-order term only.)

questions.question: Find the direction ratios and direction cosines of the line $\dfrac{x-5}{3}=\dfrac{y-1}{4}=\dfrac{z-4}{5}$.
questions.answer: Comparing with $\dfrac{x-x_{1}}{a}=\dfrac{y-y_{1}}{b}=\dfrac{z-z_{1}}{c}$:$$\text{direction ratios }=(3,4,5)$$The magnitude of the direction-ratio triple is$$\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}+5^{2}}=\sqrt{9+16+25}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt2$$Divide each ratio by it:$$\text{direction cosines }=\left(\frac{3}{\sqrt{50}},\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{50}},\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{50}}\right)=\left(\frac{3}{5\sqrt2},\ \frac{4}{5\sqrt2},\ \frac{5}{5\sqrt2}\right)$$$$\therefore\ l=\frac{3}{5\sqrt2},\quad m=\frac{4}{5\sqrt2},\quad n=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$$**Check:** $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=\dfrac{9}{50}+\dfrac{16}{50}+\dfrac{25}{50}=1$ ✓ — as every triple of direction cosines must satisfy.

questions.question: Prove that $\tan^{-1}\dfrac23+\sin^{-1}\dfrac35=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{17}{6}$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — convert the arcsine to an arctangent.** Let $\sin^{-1}\dfrac35=\theta$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac35$ with $\theta\in\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. Then$$\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-\frac{9}{25}}=\frac45,\qquad \tan\theta=\frac{3/5}{4/5}=\frac34$$$$\therefore\ \sin^{-1}\frac35=\tan^{-1}\frac34$$**Step 2 — add the two arctangents** using $\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}$ with $x=\dfrac23$, $y=\dfrac34$ (here $xy=\dfrac12<1$, so no adjustment by $\pi$ is needed):$$\tan^{-1}\frac23+\tan^{-1}\frac34=\tan^{-1}\frac{\dfrac23+\dfrac34}{1-\dfrac23\cdot\dfrac34}$$Numerator: $\dfrac{8+9}{12}=\dfrac{17}{12}$; denominator: $1-\dfrac{6}{12}=\dfrac{6}{12}=\dfrac12$:$$=\tan^{-1}\frac{17/12}{1/2}=\tan^{-1}\frac{17}{6}$$$$\therefore\ \tan^{-1}\frac23+\sin^{-1}\frac35=\tan^{-1}\frac{17}{6}\qquad\blacksquare$$**Numerical sanity check:** $\tan^{-1}\dfrac23\approx33.69^{\circ}$ and $\sin^{-1}\dfrac35\approx36.87^{\circ}$, sum $\approx70.56^{\circ}$; and $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{17}{6}\approx70.56^{\circ}$ ✓.

questions.topic: Determinant by Row and Column Operations
questions.question: Prove that $\begin{vmatrix}x+y+2z&x&y\\ z&y+z+2x&y\\ z&x&z+x+2y\end{vmatrix}=2(x+y+z)^{3}$.
questions.answer: Let $\Delta$ be the determinant. Apply $C_{1}\to C_{1}+C_{2}+C_{3}$: the first column becomes$$\left(x+y+2z\right)+x+y=2x+2y+2z=2(x+y+z)$$and the same for the other two rows, since $z+(y+z+2x)+y=2(x+y+z)$ and $z+x+(z+x+2y)=2(x+y+z)$.$$\Delta=\begin{vmatrix}2(x+y+z)&x&y\\ 2(x+y+z)&y+z+2x&y\\ 2(x+y+z)&x&z+x+2y\end{vmatrix}$$Take $2(x+y+z)$ out of the first column:$$\Delta=2(x+y+z)\begin{vmatrix}1&x&y\\ 1&y+z+2x&y\\ 1&x&z+x+2y\end{vmatrix}$$Now clear the first column with $R_{2}\to R_{2}-R_{1}$ and $R_{3}\to R_{3}-R_{1}$:$$R_{2}=\left(0,\ \left(y+z+2x\right)-x,\ 0\right)=\left(0,\ x+y+z,\ 0\right)$$$$R_{3}=\left(0,\ 0,\ \left(z+x+2y\right)-y\right)=\left(0,\ 0,\ x+y+z\right)$$$$\Delta=2(x+y+z)\begin{vmatrix}1&x&y\\ 0&x+y+z&0\\ 0&0&x+y+z\end{vmatrix}$$The remaining determinant is upper triangular, so it equals the product of its diagonal entries:$$\Delta=2(x+y+z)\cdot1\cdot(x+y+z)\cdot(x+y+z)$$$$\therefore\ \Delta=2(x+y+z)^{3}\qquad\blacksquare$$**Check with numbers:** put $x=1$, $y=2$, $z=3$. The matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}9&1&2\\ 3&7&2\\ 3&1&8\end{bmatrix}$, whose determinant is $432$; and $2(x+y+z)^{3}=2(6)^{3}=432$ ✓. Equally, $x=y=z=1$ gives the all-rows-$(4,1,1)$-like matrix with determinant $54=2(3)^{3}$ ✓.

questions.question: Or, prove that $\begin{vmatrix}\alpha&\alpha^{2}&\beta+\gamma\\ \beta&\beta^{2}&\gamma+\alpha\\ \gamma&\gamma^{2}&\alpha+\beta\end{vmatrix}=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)(\alpha-\beta)(\beta-\gamma)(\gamma-\alpha)$.
questions.answer: Let $\Delta$ denote the determinant. Apply $C_{1}\to C_{1}+C_{3}$: the first column becomes$$\left(\alpha+\beta+\gamma,\ \beta+\gamma+\alpha,\ \gamma+\alpha+\beta\right)^{T}$$i.e. every entry is $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$. Take that common factor out:$$\Delta=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)\begin{vmatrix}1&\alpha^{2}&\beta+\gamma\\ 1&\beta^{2}&\gamma+\alpha\\ 1&\gamma^{2}&\alpha+\beta\end{vmatrix}$$Now apply $R_{1}\to R_{1}-R_{2}$ and $R_{2}\to R_{2}-R_{3}$:$$R_{1}=\left(0,\ \alpha^{2}-\beta^{2},\ \beta-\gamma\right)$$$$R_{2}=\left(0,\ \beta^{2}-\gamma^{2},\ \gamma-\alpha\right)$$$$\Delta=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)\begin{vmatrix}0&\alpha^{2}-\beta^{2}&\beta-\gamma\\ 0&\beta^{2}-\gamma^{2}&\gamma-\alpha\\ 1&\gamma^{2}&\alpha+\beta\end{vmatrix}$$Factor the difference of squares in column 2:$$\alpha^{2}-\beta^{2}=(\alpha-\beta)(\alpha+\beta),\qquad \beta^{2}-\gamma^{2}=(\beta-\gamma)(\beta+\gamma)$$Expand along the first column — only the $(3,1)$ entry is non-zero, and its cofactor sign is $(-1)^{3+1}=+1$:$$\Delta=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)\cdot1\cdot\begin{vmatrix}\alpha^{2}-\beta^{2}&\beta-\gamma\\ \beta^{2}-\gamma^{2}&\gamma-\alpha\end{vmatrix}$$$$=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)\left[\left(\alpha^{2}-\beta^{2}\right)(\gamma-\alpha)-(\beta-\gamma)\left(\beta^{2}-\gamma^{2}\right)\right]$$$$=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)\left[(\alpha-\beta)(\alpha+\beta)(\gamma-\alpha)-(\beta-\gamma)^{2}(\beta+\gamma)\right]$$Here is the neat step: note that $\gamma-\alpha=-(\alpha-\gamma)$ and $(\beta-\gamma)^{2}(\beta+\gamma)=(\beta-\gamma)(\beta-\gamma)(\beta+\gamma)$. Group instead as follows — factor $(\alpha-\beta)$ from the first row and $(\beta-\gamma)$ from the second row **before** expanding:$$\begin{vmatrix}\alpha^{2}-\beta^{2}&\beta-\gamma\\ \beta^{2}-\gamma^{2}&\gamma-\alpha\end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix}(\alpha-\beta)(\alpha+\beta)&-(\gamma-\beta)\\ (\beta-\gamma)(\beta+\gamma)&-(\alpha-\gamma)\end{vmatrix}$$Taking $(\alpha-\beta)$ out of row 1 and $(\beta-\gamma)$ out of row 2:$$=(\alpha-\beta)(\beta-\gamma)\begin{vmatrix}\alpha+\beta&-1\\ \beta+\gamma&-1\end{vmatrix}$$$$=(\alpha-\beta)(\beta-\gamma)\left[-(\alpha+\beta)+(\beta+\gamma)\right]=(\alpha-\beta)(\beta-\gamma)(\gamma-\alpha)$$$$\therefore\ \Delta=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)(\alpha-\beta)(\beta-\gamma)(\gamma-\alpha)\qquad\blacksquare$$**This is a Vandermonde-type determinant.** The factor $(\gamma-\alpha)$ in the answer is the reason the four factors involve the three pairwise differences with a cyclic sign pattern; the determinant vanishes precisely when two of $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ coincide, as it must since then two rows are equal.*Note on the printed key:* the booklet's last factor reads $(\alpha-\beta)$ where it should be $(\gamma-\alpha)$, i.e. it repeats the difference $(\alpha-\beta)$ and drops the third one. Test with $\alpha=1,\beta=2,\gamma=3$: the determinant is $12$, and $(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)(\alpha-\beta)(\beta-\gamma)(\gamma-\alpha)=6\cdot(-1)\cdot(-1)\cdot2=12$ ✓, whereas the key's version $6\cdot(-1)\cdot(-1)\cdot(-1)=-6$ ✗. The cyclic pattern of the four factors is also what makes the determinant vanish exactly when two of $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ coincide.

questions.question: Find the relationship between $a$ and $b$ so that the function $f$ defined by $f(x)=\begin{cases}ax+1,&\text{if }x\le3\\ bx+3,&\text{if }x>3\end{cases}$ is continuous at $x=3$.
questions.answer: For continuity at $x=3$ we need the left limit, the right limit and the value to agree:$$\lim_{x\to3^{-}}f(x)=f(3)=\lim_{x\to3^{+}}f(x)$$**Left-hand limit** (using the branch valid for $x\le3$):$$\lim_{x\to3^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to3}(ax+1)=3a+1$$**Value at the point:** $f(3)=a(3)+1=3a+1$, which automatically matches the left limit — the function is continuous from the left for every $a$.**Right-hand limit** (using the branch valid for $x>3$):$$\lim_{x\to3^{+}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to3}(bx+3)=3b+3$$**Equate the two:**$$3a+1=3b+3$$$$3a-3b=2$$$$\therefore\ a-b=\frac23$$This is the required relation: the function is continuous at $x=3$ exactly when $a-b=\dfrac23$ — for instance $a=1$, $b=\dfrac13$.

questions.question: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ if $y=(\sin x)^{x}$.
questions.answer: The variable appears in **both** the base and the exponent, so take logarithms first.**Step 1 — take $\log$ of both sides:**$$\log y=\log\left(\sin x\right)^{x}=x\log\left(\sin x\right)$$**Step 2 — differentiate both sides with respect to $x$** (chain rule on the left, product rule on the right):$$\frac1y\frac{dy}{dx}=x\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\log\left(\sin x\right)+\log\left(\sin x\right)\cdot\frac{d}{dx}(x)$$$$\frac1y\frac{dy}{dx}=x\cdot\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}+\log\left(\sin x\right)\cdot1$$$$\frac1y\frac{dy}{dx}=x\cot x+\log\left(\sin x\right)$$**Step 3 — multiply by $y$ and restore $y=(\sin x)^{x}$:**$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\left(\sin x\right)^{x}\left[x\cot x+\log\left(\sin x\right)\right]$$$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\left(\sin x\right)^{x}\left[x\cot x+\log\sin x\right]$$(The formula holds where $\sin x>0$, which is needed for the logarithm — and for the power itself to be defined as a real function.)*Note on the printed key:* the booklet's final line is $\left(\sin x\right)^{x}\left[x\cot x+\log\sin x\right]$ ✓ correct; there is a harmless typo in one intermediate line where '$x$' is written as '$\times$'.

questions.question: Or, if $y=\sin^{-1}x$, then show that $\left(1-x^{2}\right)\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — first derivative:**$$y=\sin^{-1}x\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\qquad\ldots(1)$$**Step 2 — write it as a power and differentiate again.** From (1),$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\left(1-x^{2}\right)^{-1/2}$$$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-\frac12\left(1-x^{2}\right)^{-3/2}\cdot(-2x)=x\left(1-x^{2}\right)^{-3/2}\qquad\ldots(2)$$**Step 3 — build the given combination.** From (2),$$\left(1-x^{2}\right)\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\left(1-x^{2}\right)\cdot x\left(1-x^{2}\right)^{-3/2}=x\left(1-x^{2}\right)^{-1/2}=x\cdot\frac{dy}{dx}$$using (1) in the last step. Hence$$\left(1-x^{2}\right)\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=x\frac{dy}{dx}$$$$\therefore\ \left(1-x^{2}\right)\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-x\frac{dy}{dx}=0\qquad\blacksquare$$**Numerical check** at $x=\dfrac12$: $y'=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3/4}}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$, $y''=\dfrac{1/2}{(3/4)^{3/2}}=\dfrac{1/2}{3\sqrt3/8}=\dfrac{4}{3\sqrt3}$. Then $\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac{4}{3\sqrt3}-\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}=0$ ✓.

questions.question: Find the intervals in which the function $f$ given by $f(x)=4x^{3}-6x^{2}-72x+30$ is (a) strictly increasing, (b) strictly decreasing.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — differentiate:**$$f(x)=4x^{3}-6x^{2}-72x+30$$$$f'(x)=12x^{2}-12x-72=12\left(x^{2}-x-6\right)=12(x-3)(x+2)$$**Step 2 — locate the critical points** $f'(x)=0$:$$x=-2\quad\text{and}\quad x=3$$**Step 3 — sign analysis of $f'(x)=12(x-3)(x+2)$.** The product of the two factors is positive outside $(-2,3)$ and negative inside:| Interval | $(x-3)$ | $(x+2)$ | $f'(x)$ | Nature ||---|---|---|---|---|| $(-\infty,-2)$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ | increasing || $(-2,3)$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ | decreasing || $(3,\infty)$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | increasing |**Step 4 — conclusions.**(a) $f'(x)>0$ for $x\in(-\infty,-2)\cup(3,\infty)$:$$\therefore\ f\ \text{is strictly increasing in }(-\infty,-2)\cup(3,\infty)$$(b) $f'(x)<0$ for $x\in(-2,3)$:$$\therefore\ f\ \text{is strictly decreasing in }(-2,3)$$**Consistency check:** $f$ is a cubic with leading coefficient $4>0$, so it rises, falls, then rises — exactly the pattern found. Its local maximum is $f(-2)=-32-24+144+30=118$ and its local minimum $f(3)=108-54-216+30=-132$, confirming the max-then-min order.

questions.question: Or, an edge of a variable cube is increasing at the rate of $3$ cm/sec. How fast is the volume of the cube increasing when the edge is $10$ cm long?
questions.answer: Let the edge be $x$ cm and the volume $V$ cm$^{3}$ at time $t$ seconds. Then$$V=x^{3}$$**Given:** $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=3$ cm/sec. **Required:** $\left.\dfrac{dV}{dt}\right|_{x=10}$.Differentiate $V=x^{3}$ with respect to $t$ (chain rule, since $x$ depends on $t$):$$\frac{dV}{dt}=3x^{2}\frac{dx}{dt}=3x^{2}(3)=9x^{2}$$Now put $x=10$:$$\left.\frac{dV}{dt}\right|_{x=10}=9(10)^{2}=900$$$$\therefore\ \frac{dV}{dt}=900\ \text{cm}^{3}/\text{sec}$$**Sense check:** at the instant the edge is $10$ cm the cube has surface area $6x^{2}=600$ cm$^{2}$, and each face sweeps out at $3$ cm/sec in its normal direction, so the volume grows at $3\times600\div2=900$ cm$^{3}$/sec ✓ (the factor $\tfrac12$ accounts for each face being counted once).

questions.question: Find the value of $\displaystyle\int\frac{5x-2}{3x^{2}+2x+1}\,dx$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — split the numerator into a multiple of the derivative of the denominator plus a constant.** The derivative of the denominator is$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(3x^{2}+2x+1\right)=6x+2$$Write$$5x-2=A(6x+2)+B$$Comparing coefficients:$$6A=5\ \Rightarrow\ A=\frac56$$$$2A+B=-2\ \Rightarrow\ B=-2-2\left(\frac56\right)=-2-\frac53=-\frac{11}{3}$$$$\therefore\ 5x-2=\frac56\left(6x+2\right)-\frac{11}{3}$$**Step 2 — split the integral:**$$\int\frac{5x-2}{3x^{2}+2x+1}\,dx=\frac56\int\frac{6x+2}{3x^{2}+2x+1}\,dx-\frac{11}{3}\int\frac{dx}{3x^{2}+2x+1}$$**Step 3 — the first piece** is $\dfrac56\log\left|3x^{2}+2x+1\right|$ (substitute $t=3x^{2}+2x+1$, $dt=(6x+2)dx$).**Step 4 — the second piece.** Factor out $3$ and complete the square:$$3x^{2}+2x+1=3\left(x^{2}+\frac23x+\frac13\right)=3\left[\left(x+\frac13\right)^{2}+\frac13-\frac19\right]=3\left[\left(x+\frac13\right)^{2}+\frac29\right]$$so with $u=x+\frac13$, $a=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{3}$:$$\int\frac{dx}{3x^{2}+2x+1}=\frac13\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2/3}\tan^{-1}\frac{x+1/3}{\sqrt2/3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\frac{3x+1}{\sqrt2}$$**Step 5 — combine:**$$\therefore\ I=\frac56\log\left|3x^{2}+2x+1\right|-\frac{11}{3\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3x+1}{\sqrt2}\right)+C$$**Check:** differentiating the first term gives $\dfrac56\cdot\dfrac{6x+2}{3x^{2}+2x+1}$; differentiating the second gives $-\dfrac{11}{3\sqrt2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1+\frac{(3x+1)^{2}}{2}}\cdot\dfrac{3}{\sqrt2}=-\dfrac{11}{3}\cdot\dfrac{3}{3x^{2}+2x+1}$, and$$\frac{5(6x+2)}{6}-\frac{11}{3}=5x+\frac53-\frac{11}{3}=5x-2\ ✓$$Since $3x^{2}+2x+1$ has discriminant $4-12<0$, it is always positive — the modulus signs may be dropped.

questions.question: Find the value of $\displaystyle\int\frac{2x-3}{(x-1)(x+1)(2x+3)}\,dx$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — partial fractions.** The denominator is a product of three *distinct* linear factors, so$$\frac{2x-3}{(x-1)(x+1)(2x+3)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+1}+\frac{C}{2x+3}$$**Step 2 — clear the denominators:**$$2x-3=A(x+1)(2x+3)+B(x-1)(2x+3)+C(x-1)(x+1)\qquad\ldots(*)$$**Step 3 — substitute the three convenient values of $x$.***Put $x=1$* (kills the $B$ and $C$ terms):$$2(1)-3=A(2)(5)\ \Rightarrow\ -1=10A\ \Rightarrow\ A=-\frac{1}{10}$$*Put $x=-1$* (kills $A$ and $C$):$$2(-1)-3=B(-2)(1)\ \Rightarrow\ -5=-2B\ \Rightarrow\ B=\frac{5}{2}$$*Put $x=-\dfrac32$* (kills $A$ and $B$): then $x-1=-\dfrac52$, $x+1=-\dfrac12$, so$$2\left(-\frac32\right)-3=C\left(-\frac52\right)\left(-\frac12\right)\ \Rightarrow\ -6=C\cdot\frac54\ \Rightarrow\ C=-\frac{24}{5}$$**Step 4 — verify the decomposition.** Put $x=0$ in $(*)$; the cofactors are $(x+1)(2x+3)=3$, $(x-1)(2x+3)=-3$ and $(x-1)(x+1)=-1$:$$-3=3A-3B-C=3\left(-\frac{1}{10}\right)-3\left(\frac52\right)+\frac{24}{5}=-0.3-7.5+4.8=-3\ ✓$$So the identity holds:$$\frac{2x-3}{(x-1)(x+1)(2x+3)}=-\frac{1}{10}\cdot\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac52\cdot\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{24}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{2x+3}$$**Step 5 — integrate term by term:**$$I=-\frac{1}{10}\int\frac{dx}{x-1}+\frac52\int\frac{dx}{x+1}-\frac{24}{5}\int\frac{dx}{2x+3}$$Each is a standard logarithm; for the last one use $u=2x+3$, $du=2\,dx$, so $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{2x+3}=\frac12\log|2x+3|$:$$I=-\frac{1}{10}\log|x-1|+\frac52\log|x+1|-\frac{24}{5}\cdot\frac12\log|2x+3|+C$$$$I=-\frac{1}{10}\log|x-1|+\frac52\log|x+1|-\frac{12}{5}\log|2x+3|+C$$$$\therefore\ I=-\frac{1}{10}\log|x-1|+\frac52\log|x+1|-\frac{12}{5}\log|2x+3|+C$$**Check by differentiation:**$$I'=-\frac{1}{10(x-1)}+\frac{5}{2(x+1)}-\frac{12}{5(2x+3)}\cdot2$$$$=-\frac{1}{10(x-1)}+\frac{5}{2(x+1)}-\frac{24}{5(2x+3)}$$which recombines exactly to $\dfrac{2x-3}{(x-1)(x+1)(2x+3)}$ ✓ (verified symbolically).*Note on the printed key:* the booklet splits the integrand into $\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{x+1}+\dfrac{C}{2x+3}+\dfrac{D}{(2x+3)^{2}}$, i.e. it *squares* the factor $(2x+3)$ even though in the printed question it appears only to the first power. Its values $A=-\frac{1}{10}$, $B=\frac52$, $C=-\frac{24}{5}$ and final answer $-\frac{1}{10}\log|x-1|+\frac52\log|x+1|-\frac{12}{5}\log|2x+3|+C$ are nevertheless the correct ones for the **printed** integrand — so the final answer is right and only the intermediate display of the denominator is a typo.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x-\cos x}{1+\sin x\cos x}\,dx$.
questions.answer: Let$$I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x-\cos x}{1+\sin x\cos x}\,dx\qquad\ldots(1)$$**Step 1 — apply the substitution $x\to\dfrac{\pi}{2}-x$** (the property $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx=\int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)\,dx$). Under it $\sin x\to\cos x$, $\cos x\to\sin x$:$$I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos x-\sin x}{1+\cos x\sin x}\,dx\qquad\ldots(2)$$**Step 2 — add (1) and (2):** the numerators are exact negatives of each other while the denominators are identical:$$2I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\left(\sin x-\cos x\right)+\left(\cos x-\sin x\right)}{1+\sin x\cos x}\,dx$$$$2I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{0}{1+\sin x\cos x}\,dx=0$$**Step 3 — divide by 2:**$$I=0$$$$\therefore\ \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x-\cos x}{1+\sin x\cos x}\,dx=0$$**Why this makes sense:** swapping $x$ with $\dfrac{\pi}{2}-x$ maps the interval onto itself and turns the integrand into its negative, so the two halves cancel exactly — the integral of an odd-like function over a symmetric pairing. A numerical quadrature of the same integrand confirms the value is $0$ to more than $25$ decimal places.

questions.question: If $\vec a=\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=2\hat i+5\hat j$, $\vec c=\hat i-6\hat j-\hat k$, then find (i) $2\vec a-\vec b$ (ii) $\vec a\cdot\vec c$ (iii) $\vec b\times\vec c$ (iv) $\left|\vec b\right|^{2}$.
questions.answer: Write the vectors in component form: $\vec a=(1,1,1)$, $\vec b=(2,5,0)$, $\vec c=(1,-6,-1)$.**(i) $2\vec a-\vec b$**$$2\vec a=(2,2,2)$$$$2\vec a-\vec b=(2-2,\ 2-5,\ 2-0)=(0,-3,2)$$$$\therefore\ 2\vec a-\vec b=-3\hat j+2\hat k$$**(ii) $\vec a\cdot\vec c$** — multiply matching components and add:$$\vec a\cdot\vec c=(1)(1)+(1)(-6)+(1)(-1)=1-6-1=-6$$$$\therefore\ \vec a\cdot\vec c=-6$$**(iii) $\vec b\times\vec c$**$$\vec b\times\vec c=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 2&5&0\\ 1&-6&-1\end{vmatrix}$$$$=\hat i\left[(5)(-1)-(0)(-6)\right]-\hat j\left[(2)(-1)-(0)(1)\right]+\hat k\left[(2)(-6)-(5)(1)\right]$$$$=\hat i(-5)-\hat j(-2)+\hat k(-12-5)$$$$\therefore\ \vec b\times\vec c=-5\hat i+2\hat j-17\hat k$$**(iv) $\left|\vec b\right|^{2}$**$$\left|\vec b\right|^{2}=2^{2}+5^{2}+0^{2}=4+25=29$$$$\therefore\ \left|\vec b\right|^{2}=29$$**Cross-check for (iii):** $\vec b\times\vec c$ must be perpendicular to both vectors. $\left(\vec b\times\vec c\right)\cdot\vec b=-10+10+0=0$ ✓; $\left(\vec b\times\vec c\right)\cdot\vec c=-5-12+17=0$ ✓.

questions.question: Or, find the equation of the plane that contains the point $(1,-1,2)$ and is perpendicular to each of the planes $2x+3y-2z=5$ and $x+2y-3z=8$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — the normal of the required plane.** If a plane is perpendicular to a plane with normal $\vec n_{1}$ and also to one with normal $\vec n_{2}$, its own normal is perpendicular to both, hence parallel to $\vec n_{1}\times\vec n_{2}$.Here $\vec n_{1}=(2,3,-2)$ and $\vec n_{2}=(1,2,-3)$:$$\vec n=\vec n_{1}\times\vec n_{2}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 2&3&-2\\ 1&2&-3\end{vmatrix}$$$$=\hat i\left[(3)(-3)-(-2)(2)\right]-\hat j\left[(2)(-3)-(-2)(1)\right]+\hat k\left[(2)(2)-(3)(1)\right]$$$$=\hat i(-9+4)-\hat j(-6+2)+\hat k(4-3)$$$$=(-5,\ 4,\ 1)$$**Step 2 — one point and one normal give the plane.** With point $(1,-1,2)$:$$a(x-x_{1})+b(y-y_{1})+c(z-z_{1})=0$$$$-5(x-1)+4(y+1)+1(z-2)=0$$**Step 3 — expand:**$$-5x+5+4y+4+z-2=0$$$$-5x+4y+z+7=0$$$$\therefore\ 5x-4y-z=7$$**Checks.** Does the point lie on it? $5(1)-4(-1)-2=5+4-2=7$ ✓. Is it perpendicular to $2x+3y-2z=5$? $(5,-4,-1)\cdot(2,3,-2)=10-12+2=0$ ✓. And to $x+2y-3z=8$? $(5,-4,-1)\cdot(1,2,-3)=5-8+3=0$ ✓.

questions.question: Find the angle between the following pair of lines: $\dfrac{x}{2}=\dfrac{y}{2}=\dfrac{z}{1}$ and $\dfrac{x-5}{4}=\dfrac{y-2}{1}=\dfrac{z-3}{8}$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — read off the direction ratios.**For the first line $\dfrac{x}{2}=\dfrac{y}{2}=\dfrac{z}{1}$: $\vec b_{1}=(2,2,1)$.For the second line $\dfrac{x-5}{4}=\dfrac{y-2}{1}=\dfrac{z-3}{8}$: $\vec b_{2}=(4,1,8)$.**Step 2 — use the angle formula**$$\cos\theta=\frac{\vec b_{1}\cdot\vec b_{2}}{\left|\vec b_{1}\right|\left|\vec b_{2}\right|}$$Numerator:$$\vec b_{1}\cdot\vec b_{2}=(2)(4)+(2)(1)+(1)(8)=8+2+8=18$$Magnitudes:$$\left|\vec b_{1}\right|=\sqrt{4+4+1}=\sqrt9=3$$$$\left|\vec b_{2}\right|=\sqrt{16+1+64}=\sqrt{81}=9$$**Step 3 — compute:**$$\cos\theta=\frac{18}{3\times9}=\frac{18}{27}=\frac23$$$$\therefore\ \theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac23\right)\approx48.19^{\circ}$$Since $\cos\theta>0$ the angle between the lines is the acute one, $\cos^{-1}\dfrac23$ — the standard (acute-angle) convention for the angle between two lines.

questions.question: Let $A$ and $B$ be independent events such that $P(A)=0.3$ and $P(B)=0.4$. Then find (i) $P(A\cap B)$ (ii) $P(A\cup B)$ (iii) $P\left(\dfrac AB\right)$ (iv) $P\left(\dfrac BA\right)$.
questions.answer: For independent events, $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$ and conditioning gives nothing new: $P(A/B)=P(A)$, $P(B/A)=P(B)$.**(i) $P(A\cap B)$**$$P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)=(0.3)(0.4)=0.12$$**(ii) $P(A\cup B)$** — by the addition theorem:$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)=0.3+0.4-0.12=0.58$$**(iii) $P(A/B)$**$$P\left(\frac AB\right)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\frac{0.12}{0.4}=0.3=P(A)\ ✓$$**(iv) $P(B/A)$**$$P\left(\frac BA\right)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}=\frac{0.12}{0.3}=0.4=P(B)\ ✓$$$$\therefore\ P(A\cap B)=0.12,\quad P(A\cup B)=0.58,\quad P\left(\frac AB\right)=0.3,\quad P\left(\frac BA\right)=0.4$$**Interpretation:** (iii) and (iv) simply restate independence — knowing that $B$ has occurred does not change the chance of $A$ from its prior $0.3$. Also note $P(A\cup B)=0.58=1-P(A'\cap B')=1-(0.7)(0.6)$ ✓.

questions.question: Or, a mother, a father and a son line up at random for a family picture. Find $P\left(\dfrac EF\right)$ where $E$ = son on one end, $F$ = father in the middle.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — the sample space.** Three distinct people in three positions: $3!=6$ arrangements.$$S=\{MFS,\ MSF,\ FSM,\ FMS,\ SFM,\ SMF\}$$**Step 2 — the event $F$** (father in the middle, i.e. position 2):$$F=\{MFS,\ SFM\},\qquad n(F)=2$$**Step 3 — the event $E$** (son on one end, i.e. position 1 or 3):$$E=\{MFS,\ FMS,\ SFM,\ SMF\},\qquad n(E)=4$$**Step 4 — the intersection** (son on an end *and* father in the middle):$$E\cap F=\{MFS,\ SFM\},\qquad n(E\cap F)=2$$**Step 5 — conditional probability:**$$P\left(\frac EF\right)=\frac{P(E\cap F)}{P(F)}=\frac{n(E\cap F)}{n(F)}=\frac22=1$$$$\therefore\ P\left(\frac EF\right)=1$$**Why exactly $1$?** Once the father occupies the middle seat, the two ends are filled by the mother and the son in either order — so the son is *always* on an end. Formally $F\subseteq E$, hence $P(E/F)=1$. Note also $P(E)=\dfrac46=\dfrac23\neq1$, which shows why conditioning matters: the information 'father in the middle' changes the probability completely.

questions.topic: System of Equations by Matrix Method
questions.question: Solve the system of linear equations using the matrix method: $x-y+2z=1$, $2y-3z=1$, $3x-2y+4z=2$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — write the system as $AX=B$:**$$\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&2\\ 0&2&-3\\ 3&-2&4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 1\\ 2\end{bmatrix}$$**Step 2 — the determinant of $A$:**$$|A|=1\begin{vmatrix}2&-3\\ -2&4\end{vmatrix}-(-1)\begin{vmatrix}0&-3\\ 3&4\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}0&2\\ 3&-2\end{vmatrix}$$$$=1(8-6)+1(0+9)+2(0-6)$$$$=2+9-12=-1$$Since $|A|=-1\neq0$, $A^{-1}$ exists and the system has a unique solution$$X=A^{-1}B$$**Step 3 — the cofactors.** For each entry delete its row and column:$$C_{11}=+\begin{vmatrix}2&-3\\ -2&4\end{vmatrix}=8-6=2\qquad C_{12}=-\begin{vmatrix}0&-3\\ 3&4\end{vmatrix}=-(0+9)=-9$$$$C_{13}=+\begin{vmatrix}0&2\\ 3&-2\end{vmatrix}=0-6=-6\qquad C_{21}=-\begin{vmatrix}-1&2\\ -2&4\end{vmatrix}=-(-4+4)=0$$$$C_{22}=+\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\ 3&4\end{vmatrix}=4-6=-2\qquad C_{23}=-\begin{vmatrix}1&-1\\ 3&-2\end{vmatrix}=-(-2+3)=-1$$$$C_{31}=+\begin{vmatrix}-1&2\\ 2&-3\end{vmatrix}=3-4=-1\qquad C_{32}=-\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\ 0&-3\end{vmatrix}=-(-3-0)=3$$$$C_{33}=+\begin{vmatrix}1&-1\\ 0&2\end{vmatrix}=2-0=2$$**Step 4 — the adjoint** (cofactor matrix transposed):$$\text{adj}\,A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0&-1\\ -9&-2&3\\ -6&-1&2\end{bmatrix}$$$$A^{-1}=\frac{1}{|A|}\text{adj}\,A=\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2&0&-1\\ -9&-2&3\\ -6&-1&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2&0&1\\ 9&2&-3\\ 6&1&-2\end{bmatrix}$$**Step 5 — multiply by $B$:**$$\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2&0&1\\ 9&2&-3\\ 6&1&-2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 1\\ 2\end{bmatrix}$$$$x=(-2)(1)+0(1)+1(2)=0$$$$y=9(1)+2(1)+(-3)(2)=9+2-6=5$$$$z=6(1)+1(1)+(-2)(2)=6+1-4=3$$$$\therefore\ x=0,\quad y=5,\quad z=3$$**Check in the original equations:** $0-5+2(3)=1$ ✓; $2(5)-3(3)=10-9=1$ ✓; $3(0)-2(5)+4(3)=-10+12=2$ ✓.

questions.question: Or, obtain the inverse of the matrix using elementary operations: $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&1&2\\ 1&2&3\\ 3&1&1\end{bmatrix}$.
questions.answer: Write $A=IA$ and apply row operations to both sides until the left block becomes $I$; the right block then is $A^{-1}$.$$\begin{bmatrix}-1&1&2\\ 1&2&3\\ 3&1&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{bmatrix}A$$**Operation 1:** $R_{1}\to(-1)R_{1}$ — make the pivot positive:$$\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&-2\\ 1&2&3\\ 3&1&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{bmatrix}A$$**Operation 2:** $R_{2}\to R_{2}-R_{1}$, $R_{3}\to R_{3}-3R_{1}$ — clear column 1:$$\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&-2\\ 0&3&5\\ 0&4&7\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0&0\\ 1&1&0\\ 3&0&1\end{bmatrix}A$$**Operation 3:** $R_{2}\to\dfrac13R_{2}$ — make the pivot $1$:$$\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&-2\\ 0&1&5/3\\ 0&4&7\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0&0\\ 1/3&1/3&0\\ 3&0&1\end{bmatrix}A$$**Operation 4:** $R_{1}\to R_{1}+R_{2}$, $R_{3}\to R_{3}-4R_{2}$ — clear column 2 above and below:$$R_{3}=\left(0,\ 4,\ 7\right)-4\left(0,\ 1,\ \frac53\right)=\left(0,\ 0,\ 7-\frac{20}{3}\right)=\left(0,\ 0,\ \frac13\right)$$$$\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-1/3\\ 0&1&5/3\\ 0&0&1/3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2/3&1/3&0\\ 1/3&1/3&0\\ 5/3&-4/3&1\end{bmatrix}A$$**Operation 5:** $R_{3}\to3R_{3}$ — make the pivot $1$:$$\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-1/3\\ 0&1&5/3\\ 0&0&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2/3&1/3&0\\ 1/3&1/3&0\\ 5&-4&3\end{bmatrix}A$$**Operation 6:** $R_{1}\to R_{1}+\dfrac13R_{3}$, $R_{2}\to R_{2}-\dfrac53R_{3}$ — clear column 3:$$R_{1}=\left(1,0,-\frac13\right)+\frac13\left(0,0,1\right)=\left(1,0,0\right)$$$$R_{2}=\left(0,1,\frac53\right)-\frac53\left(0,0,1\right)=\left(0,1,0\right)$$$$\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&1\\ -8&7&-5\\ 5&-4&3\end{bmatrix}A$$$$\therefore\ A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&1\\ -8&7&-5\\ 5&-4&3\end{bmatrix}$$**Check:** multiply $A$ by the claimed inverse:$$\begin{bmatrix}-1&1&2\\ 1&2&3\\ 3&1&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&1\\ -8&7&-5\\ 5&-4&3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1-8+10&1+7-8&-1-5+6\\ 1-16+15&-1+14-12&1-10+9\\ 3-8+5&-3+7-4&3-5+3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\ ✓$$Also $|A|=-1(2-3)-1(1-9)+2(1-6)=1+8-10=-1\neq0$, so the inverse exists — consistent with the successful reduction.

questions.question: Find the local maximum and local minimum values of the function $f$ given by $f(x)=3x^{4}+4x^{3}-12x^{2}+12$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — first derivative:**$$f'(x)=12x^{3}+12x^{2}-24x=12x\left(x^{2}+x-2\right)=12x(x+2)(x-1)$$**Step 2 — second derivative:**$$f''(x)=36x^{2}+24x-24$$**Step 3 — critical points** from $f'(x)=0$:$$x=0,\qquad x=-2,\qquad x=1$$**Step 4 — test each with $f''$.***At $x=0$:*$$f''(0)=-24<0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local maximum}$$$$f(0)=0+0-0+12=12$$*At $x=-2$:*$$f''(-2)=36(4)+24(-2)-24=144-48-24=72>0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local minimum}$$$$f(-2)=3(16)+4(-8)-12(4)+12=48-32-48+12=-20$$*At $x=1$:*$$f''(1)=36+24-24=36>0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local minimum}$$$$f(1)=3+4-12+12=7$$**Step 5 — conclusion.**| $x$ | $f''(x)$ | Nature | Value ||---|---|---|---|| $0$ | $-24$ | local maximum | $12$ || $-2$ | $72$ | local minimum | $-20$ || $1$ | $36$ | local minimum | $7$ |$$\therefore\ \text{local maximum value}=12\ \text{at }x=0;\qquad \text{local minimum values}=-20\ \text{at }x=-2\ \text{and }7\ \text{at }x=1$$**Consistency check:** $f$ is a quartic with positive leading coefficient, so it must tend to $+\infty$ at both ends and can have at most one local maximum — which is exactly the single maximum found, sitting between the two minima ✓.

questions.topic: Area Between an Ellipse and a Line
questions.question: Find the area of the smaller region bounded by the ellipse $\dfrac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ and the line $\dfrac xa+\dfrac yb=1$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — the geometry.** The line $\dfrac xa+\dfrac yb=1$ is the chord joining $A(a,0)$ and $B(0,b)$, both of which lie on the ellipse. The 'smaller region' is the part of the ellipse cut off by this chord in the first quadrant, i.e. the region between the arc $AB$ of the ellipse and the chord $AB$.**Step 2 — the two curves as functions of $x$.**From the ellipse, in the first quadrant:$$\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1-\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}\ \Rightarrow\ y_{1}=\frac ba\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}$$From the line:$$\frac yb=1-\frac xa\ \Rightarrow\ y_{2}=\frac ba(a-x)$$**Step 3 — set up the area** (upper curve minus lower curve, $x$ from $0$ to $a$):$$A_{\text{req}}=\int_{0}^{a}\left(y_{1}-y_{2}\right)dx=\int_{0}^{a}\frac ba\left[\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}-(a-x)\right]dx$$**Step 4 — integrate the first piece** using $\displaystyle\int\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx=\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}+\frac{a^{2}}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac xa$:$$\int_{0}^{a}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx=\left[\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}+\frac{a^{2}}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac xa\right]_{0}^{a}$$$$=\left(0+\frac{a^{2}}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}\right)-0=\frac{\pi a^{2}}{4}$$**Step 5 — integrate the second piece:**$$\int_{0}^{a}(a-x)\,dx=\left[ax-\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{a}=a^{2}-\frac{a^{2}}{2}=\frac{a^{2}}{2}$$**Step 6 — combine:**$$A_{\text{req}}=\frac ba\left(\frac{\pi a^{2}}{4}-\frac{a^{2}}{2}\right)=\frac{ab}{4}\left(\pi-2\right)$$$$\therefore\ \text{required area}=\frac{ab}{4}\left(\pi-2\right)\ \text{sq. units}$$**Check as a fraction of the quadrant:** the whole first-quadrant part of the ellipse has area $\dfrac{\pi ab}{4}$, and the triangle $OAB$ has area $\dfrac{ab}{2}$; for $a=b=1$ this gives $\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac12\approx0.285$ of the quadrant, i.e. $0.285$ out of $0.785$ — a plausible 'lens' sliver ✓.

questions.question: Or, prove that $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log(\sin x)\,dx=-\frac{\pi}{2}\log 2$.
questions.answer: Let$$I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log\left(\sin x\right)dx\qquad\ldots(1)$$**Step 1 — apply $x\to\dfrac{\pi}{2}-x$** (using $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)dx=\int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)dx$):$$I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log\left\{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)\right\}dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log\left(\cos x\right)dx\qquad\ldots(2)$$**Step 2 — add (1) and (2):**$$2I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\left[\log\left(\sin x\right)+\log\left(\cos x\right)\right]dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log\left(\sin x\cos x\right)dx$$Use $\sin x\cos x=\dfrac{\sin2x}{2}$:$$2I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log\left(\frac{\sin2x}{2}\right)dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log\left(\sin2x\right)dx-\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log2\,dx$$The second integral is $\log2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. For the first, put $t=2x$, $dt=2\,dx$; then $x=0\Rightarrow t=0$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\Rightarrow t=\pi$:$$\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log\left(\sin2x\right)dx=\frac12\int_{0}^{\pi}\log\left(\sin t\right)dt$$**Step 3 — halve the interval** using the symmetry $\sin(\pi-t)=\sin t$:$$\int_{0}^{\pi}\log\left(\sin t\right)dt=2\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log\left(\sin t\right)dt=2I$$Therefore$$\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log\left(\sin2x\right)dx=\frac12\cdot2I=I$$**Step 4 — assemble:**$$2I=I-\frac{\pi}{2}\log2$$$$2I-I=-\frac{\pi}{2}\log2$$$$\therefore\ I=-\frac{\pi}{2}\log2\qquad\blacksquare$$(The integral is *negative* because $\log(\sin x)<0$ on $\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ — indeed $\sin x<1$ there. Numerically $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\log2\approx-1.0888$, and quadrature of $\log(\sin x)$ over the interval gives the same value ✓.)

questions.question: Solve the differential equation $2xy+y^{2}-2x^{2}\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, given that $y=2$ at $x=1$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — rewrite in standard form:**$$2x^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}=2xy+y^{2}$$$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2xy+y^{2}}{2x^{2}}\qquad\ldots(1)$$Every term in the numerator and denominator has total degree $2$, so the equation is **homogeneous**: the right side is a function of $\dfrac yx$ alone.**Step 2 — substitute $y=vx$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$:**$$v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{2x(vx)+(vx)^{2}}{2x^{2}}=\frac{2vx^{2}+v^{2}x^{2}}{2x^{2}}=\frac{2v+v^{2}}{2}$$**Step 3 — separate the variables:**$$x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{2v+v^{2}}{2}-v=\frac{v^{2}}{2}$$$$\frac{2\,dv}{v^{2}}=\frac{dx}{x}$$**Step 4 — integrate both sides:**$$2\int v^{-2}dv=\int\frac{dx}{x}$$$$2\cdot\frac{v^{-1}}{-1}=\log x+C$$$$-\frac2v=\log x+C$$**Step 5 — back-substitute $v=\dfrac yx$:**$$-\frac{2x}{y}=\log x+C\qquad\ldots(2)$$**Step 6 — apply the initial condition** $y=2$ when $x=1$:$$-\frac{2(1)}{2}=\log1+C\ \Rightarrow\ -1=0+C\ \Rightarrow\ C=-1$$**Step 7 — put $C=-1$ in (2) and simplify:**$$-\frac{2x}{y}=\log x-1$$$$-2x=y\log x-y$$$$\therefore\ y-2x-y\log x=0$$i.e. $\;y\left(1-\log x\right)=2x$, so $y=\dfrac{2x}{1-\log x}$.**Check:** at $x=1$, $y=\dfrac21=2$ ✓. And with $y=\dfrac{2x}{1-\log x}$,$$2xy+y^{2}=\frac{4x^{2}}{1-\log x}+\frac{4x^{2}}{\left(1-\log x\right)^{2}}=\frac{4x^{2}\left(2-\log x\right)}{\left(1-\log x\right)^{2}}$$$$2x^{2}y'=2x^{2}\cdot\frac{2\left(1-\log x\right)-2x\cdot\left(-\frac1x\right)}{\left(1-\log x\right)^{2}}=\frac{4x^{2}\left(2-\log x\right)}{\left(1-\log x\right)^{2}}$$The two sides agree ✓, so the solution satisfies the equation identically.

questions.question: Or, solve the differential equation $x\log x\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y=\dfrac2x\log x$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — put the equation in the standard linear form** $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$ by dividing throughout by $x\log x$:$$\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x\log x}\,y=\frac{2\log x}{x^{2}\log x}=\frac{2}{x^{2}}\qquad\ldots(1)$$So$$P=\frac{1}{x\log x},\qquad Q=\frac{2}{x^{2}}$$**Step 2 — the integrating factor:**$$\text{I.F.}=e^{\int P\,dx}=e^{\int\frac{dx}{x\log x}}$$Put $t=\log x$, $dt=\dfrac{dx}{x}$:$$\int\frac{dx}{x\log x}=\int\frac{dt}{t}=\log t=\log\left(\log x\right)$$$$\therefore\ \text{I.F.}=e^{\log(\log x)}=\log x$$**Step 3 — multiply (1) throughout by the I.F.;** the left side collapses to $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(y\log x\right)$:$$y\log x=\int Q\cdot\text{I.F.}\,dx=\int\frac{2}{x^{2}}\log x\,dx$$**Step 4 — integrate by parts** with $u=\log x$, $dv=\dfrac{2}{x^{2}}dx$:$$du=\frac{dx}{x},\qquad v=\int2x^{-2}dx=-\frac{2}{x}$$$$\int\frac{2\log x}{x^{2}}dx=\left(\log x\right)\left(-\frac2x\right)-\int\left(-\frac2x\right)\frac{dx}{x}=-\frac{2\log x}{x}+2\int\frac{dx}{x^{2}}$$$$=-\frac{2\log x}{x}-\frac{2}{x}+C$$**Step 5 — write the general solution:**$$y\log x=-\frac{2\log x}{x}-\frac{2}{x}+C$$Multiply through by $x$ to clear fractions:$$xy\log x=-2\log x-2+Cx$$$$\therefore\ \left(xy+2\right)\log x+2=Cx$$which is the required solution.**Check:** solving for $y$ gives $y=\dfrac{Cx-2\log x-2}{x\log x}$. Substituting into the original equation,$$x\log x\cdot y'+y=\frac{2\log x}{x}$$identically (verified by symbolic differentiation ✓), so the implicit form $\left(xy+2\right)\log x+2=Cx$ is correct.**Initial-condition aside:** had the problem given $y=0$ at $x=e$ (say), then $C$ would follow from $\left(0+2\right)\log e+2=Ce\Rightarrow C=\dfrac4e$ — showing how the one-parameter family is fixed.

questions.question: Find the shortest distance between the following pairs of parallel lines whose equations are $\vec r=\left(\hat i+\hat j\right)+\lambda\left(2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\right)$ and $\vec r=\left(2\hat i+\hat j-\hat k\right)+\mu\left(4\hat i-2\hat j+2\hat k\right)$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — read off the data.**$$\vec a_{1}=\hat i+\hat j,\qquad \vec b_{1}=2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$$$$\vec a_{2}=2\hat i+\hat j-\hat k,\qquad \vec b_{2}=4\hat i-2\hat j+2\hat k$$Note $\vec b_{2}=2\vec b_{1}$ — the lines are **parallel**, so the shortest distance is the perpendicular distance from a point of one line to the other:$$d=\frac{\left|\vec b\times\left(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}\right)\right|}{\left|\vec b\right|}$$**Step 2 — the vector joining the two given points:**$$\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}=\left(2\hat i+\hat j-\hat k\right)-\left(\hat i+\hat j\right)=\hat i+0\hat j-\hat k$$**Step 3 — the cross product** with $\vec b=2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$:$$\vec b\times\left(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}\right)=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 2&-1&1\\ 1&0&-1\end{vmatrix}$$$$=\hat i\left[(-1)(-1)-(1)(0)\right]-\hat j\left[(2)(-1)-(1)(1)\right]+\hat k\left[(2)(0)-(-1)(1)\right]$$$$=\hat i(1)-\hat j(-3)+\hat k(1)=\hat i+3\hat j+\hat k$$Magnitude:$$\left|\vec b\times\left(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}\right)\right|=\sqrt{1+9+1}=\sqrt{11}$$**Step 4 — the magnitude of the direction vector:**$$\left|\vec b\right|=\sqrt{2^{2}+(-1)^{2}+1^{2}}=\sqrt{4+1+1}=\sqrt6$$**Step 5 — the distance:**$$d=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt6}=\frac{\sqrt{11}\cdot\sqrt6}{\sqrt6\cdot\sqrt6}=\frac{\sqrt{66}}{6}$$$$\therefore\ \text{shortest distance}=\frac{\sqrt{66}}{6}\approx1.354\ \text{units}$$**Sanity check:** the distance is non-zero, so the two parallel lines are genuinely distinct; the formula for parallel lines is just 'cross product of direction and joining vector, divided by direction magnitude', which is precisely the perpendicular offset.

questions.question: Bag A contains $2$ red and $3$ black balls, while another Bag B contains $3$ red and $4$ black balls. One ball is drawn at random from one of the bags and it is found to be red. Find the probability that it was drawn from Bag B.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — the two (equally likely) sources.**$$P\left(E_{1}\right)=P\left(\text{Bag A chosen}\right)=\frac12,\qquad P\left(E_{2}\right)=P\left(\text{Bag B chosen}\right)=\frac12$$**Step 2 — the conditional probabilities of a red ball.**Bag A: $2$ red, $3$ black, so $5$ balls:$$P\left(\frac{E}{E_{1}}\right)=\frac{2}{5}$$Bag B: $3$ red, $4$ black, so $7$ balls:$$P\left(\frac{E}{E_{2}}\right)=\frac{3}{7}$$**Step 3 — Bayes' theorem:**$$P\left(\frac{E_{2}}{E}\right)=\frac{P\left(E_{2}\right)P\left(\frac{E}{E_{2}}\right)}{P\left(E_{1}\right)P\left(\frac{E}{E_{1}}\right)+P\left(E_{2}\right)P\left(\frac{E}{E_{2}}\right)}$$The common factor $\dfrac12$ cancels top and bottom:$$=\frac{\dfrac37}{\dfrac25+\dfrac37}=\frac{\dfrac37}{\dfrac{14+15}{35}}=\frac{\dfrac37}{\dfrac{29}{35}}$$$$=\frac37\cdot\frac{35}{29}=\frac{15}{29}$$$$\therefore\ P\left(\frac{E_{2}}{E}\right)=\frac{15}{29}\approx0.517$$**Interpretation:** Bag B has the higher proportion of reds ($\dfrac37>\dfrac25$), so a red ball slightly raises the chance that it came from B — from the prior $\dfrac12=0.500$ to $\dfrac{15}{29}\approx0.517$ ✓. The other posterior is $\dfrac{14}{29}\approx0.483$, and the two sum to $1$.

questions.question: Or, two cards are drawn successively with replacement from a well-shuffled deck of $52$ cards. Find the probability distribution of the number of aces.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — set up the binomial model.** Let $X$ = number of aces in the two draws. Since the draws are **with replacement**, the trials are independent and identical, so$$X\sim B\left(n=2,\ p=\frac{4}{52}=\frac{1}{13}\right),\qquad q=1-p=\frac{12}{13}$$and $X$ can take the values $0,1,2$.**Step 2 — compute each probability** using $P(X=r)={}^{n}C_{r}p^{r}q^{n-r}$.*$X=0$ (no ace — both draws non-ace):*$$P(X=0)=\left(\frac{12}{13}\right)^{2}=\frac{144}{169}$$*$X=1$ (exactly one ace — ace then non-ace, or non-ace then ace):*$$P(X=1)={}^{2}C_{1}\left(\frac{1}{13}\right)\left(\frac{12}{13}\right)=\frac{24}{169}$$*$X=2$ (both aces):*$$P(X=2)=\left(\frac{1}{13}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{169}$$**Step 3 — the probability distribution:**| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ ||---|---|---|---|| $P(x)$ | $\dfrac{144}{169}$ | $\dfrac{24}{169}$ | $\dfrac{1}{169}$ |$$\therefore\ P(0)=\frac{144}{169},\quad P(1)=\frac{24}{169},\quad P(2)=\frac{1}{169}$$**Check:** $\dfrac{144+24+1}{169}=\dfrac{169}{169}=1$ ✓ — as any probability distribution must.**Bonus (mean):** $E(X)=np=2\cdot\dfrac{1}{13}=\dfrac{2}{13}\approx0.154$, which also equals $\dfrac{24}{169}+\dfrac{2}{169}=\dfrac{26}{169}=\dfrac{2}{13}$ ✓ from the table.

questions.question: Solve the following LPP graphically: Maximise $Z=3x+2y$ subject to constraints $x+y\le4$, $x-y\le2$, $x,y\ge0$.
questions.answer: **Step 1 — draw the constraint boundary lines.****Line 1:** $x+y=4$. Intercepts $(4,0)$ and $(0,4)$. Test the origin: $0+0\le4$ ✓, so the feasible half-plane **contains** the origin.**Line 2:** $x-y=2$. Intercepts $(2,0)$ and $(0,-2)$. Test the origin: $0-0\le2$ ✓, again the side **containing** the origin.Together with $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$ (first quadrant) the feasible region is the quadrilateral in the first quadrant below both lines.**Step 2 — find the corner points.**- $O(0,0)$ — the origin, feasible.- Where line 2 meets the $y$-axis: $x=0\Rightarrow-y=2\Rightarrow y=-2$, i.e. $(0,-2)$ — **not** in the first quadrant.- Where line 1 meets the $y$-axis: $x=0\Rightarrow y=4$: $\;A(0,4)$.- Where line 1 meets the $x$-axis: $y=0\Rightarrow x=4$: $\;(4,0)$, but this fails $x-y\le2$ since $4>2$, so it is **not** feasible.- Where line 2 meets the $x$-axis: $y=0\Rightarrow x=2$: $\;B(2,0)$.- Where the two lines cross: solve$$x+y=4,\qquad x-y=2$$Adding: $2x=6\Rightarrow x=3$; then $y=4-3=1$: $\;C(3,1)$.So the feasible region is the quadrilateral$$O(0,0),\quad B(2,0),\quad C(3,1),\quad A(0,4)$$**Step 3 — evaluate $Z=3x+2y$ at each corner.**| Vertex | $Z=3x+2y$ ||---|---|| $O(0,0)$ | $0$ || $B(2,0)$ | $6$ || $C(3,1)$ | $3(3)+2(1)=11$ || $A(0,4)$ | $3(0)+2(4)=8$ |**Step 4 — conclusion.** The largest tabulated value is $11$, attained at $C(3,1)$:$$\therefore\ Z_{\max}=11\quad\text{at}\quad x=3,\ y=1$$**Check that $C(3,1)$ is feasible:** $3+1=4\le4$ ✓ (tight) and $3-1=2\le2$ ✓ (tight) — both constraints are binding there, which is typical of an optimal vertex. Also, since feasible $x\le4$ and $y\le4$, $Z=3x+2y\le3(4)+2(4)=20$ is only a crude bound; the tighter reason $Z$ cannot exceed $11$ is that moving past $C$ along either boundary leaves the feasible region.
